opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real connection there, though it's not automatic. When you train models in multi-agent settings where they have to cooperate, a few skills get forced into existence that matter a lot for working with people too.

The first is modeling what the other party knows and doesn't know. If two agents are splitting up a task and one has information the other lacks, the one that does well learns to communicate the right things at the right time. It doesn't dump everything, and it doesn't assume shared context that isn't there. That's basically the core of being a good collaborator with a human. A lot of the frustration people have with models today is that they either over-explain or skip steps, because they're not tracking what you actually have in your head.

The second is handling ambiguity and asking for clarification. In cooperative games, agents often learn that a quick check-in is cheaper than going down the wrong path. With people, knowing when to ask versus when to just proceed is one of the hardest calibration problems, and you can get some pressure on it in agent-to-agent settings.

The third is adapting to a partner instead of to a fixed environment. A model trained only against static benchmarks learns to optimize a task. A model trained alongside other agents with different styles and capabilities has to learn conventions and adjust to whoever it's working with. That flexibility is closer to what you need when the "other agent" is a person with their own preferences and quirks.

The big caveat is that agents can develop conventions that work great among themselves but are completely alien to humans: shorthand, weird protocols, things that are efficient but illegible. So you can't just do self-play and expect it to transfer. You need some anchor to human behavior, whether that's training with human data, mixing in human partners, or explicitly rewarding legibility. My view is that multi-agent cooperation is a useful scaffold for building those collaborative instincts, but the target always has to be humans, not other copies of the model.

r001.rationale: It describes agents cooperating in multi-agent settings, but does not propose jointly training multiple agents specifically to simulate interactions among multiple people.

r002.rationale: It calls multi-agent cooperation a useful scaffold for collaborative instincts and explains how those skills could transfer to working with people, with a human-focused caveat.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, actually. So the way I'd frame it is: when you train models to work together on a task, you're really forcing them to learn a bunch of skills that have nothing to do with the task itself and everything to do with communication. Like, one model has to figure out what the other one knows and doesn't know. It has to decide what information is worth sending and what's noise. It has to notice when the other agent is confused and go back and clarify. And it has to build some representation of "what is this other party trying to do, and how does what I'm doing fit into that."

And those are exactly the things that make a model useful to a person. The failure modes we see with assistants today are mostly not "the model couldn't solve the problem." They're things like the model didn't ask the obvious clarifying question, or it buried the one important point under five paragraphs of hedging, or it just didn't realize the user had a different goal than the one it assumed. Those are theory-of-mind and communication failures, and multi-agent training is a pretty natural way to put pressure on exactly those.

The nice thing about the agent-to-agent setting is you can scale it. Getting a human in the loop for every interaction is expensive and slow, but two models can run millions of episodes against each other, and you can build environments where cooperation is actually required to succeed — where neither one has all the information, so they have to communicate well or they fail.

Now, I'd put a big caveat on it. Models cooperating with models is not the same as models cooperating with people. Models can develop their own shorthand, their own weird conventions, things that are super efficient between two copies of the same network and completely illegible to a human. So you have to be deliberate about keeping the communication grounded — keep it in natural language, make sure a human could follow along, maybe mix in actual human feedback so the thing doesn't drift into some private language. If you do that, I think it's a genuinely promising path. If you don't, you just get models that are very good at talking to themselves.

r002.rationale: It says model-to-model cooperation builds communication and perspective-taking skills useful with people, and calls multi-agent training a promising path.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that cooperation forces you to deal with another agent whose goals and information may differ from yours. You have to figure out what they’re trying to do, communicate what you know, and coordinate your actions. Those are also things we want an AI system to do when it works with a person.

You could imagine a task where two models each have some information, but neither can solve the problem alone. To succeed, they need to ask useful questions and recognize when the other model knows something they don’t. That’s potentially a way to train behaviors that are useful in human collaboration, too.

The caveat is that models could learn to cooperate in ways that don’t work very well for people. So I’d think of model-to-model cooperation as a training ground. You’d still need to test whether those skills transfer to working with humans—whether the model understands your intent, explains itself clearly, and responds appropriately when you correct it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hope is that cooperation forces models to practice some of the skills that are also important when working with people. You have to figure out what your partner knows, what they’re trying to do, and how your actions fit with theirs. And you have to communicate when you’re uncertain or when you need help.

With other AI agents, we can create situations where those skills are necessary and study whether they actually emerge. For example, you can give two agents different information, so neither can solve the task alone. Then success depends on sharing the right information and using what the other agent tells you.

But there’s an important gap between cooperating with another copy of yourself and cooperating with a person. People have different expectations, different ways of communicating, and goals that aren’t always explicit. So I’d view AI-to-AI cooperation as a useful training environment, but the real test is whether those behaviors transfer to working with people—especially people the model hasn’t encountered during training.

r001.rationale: The response describes using two AI agents to practice cooperation, but does not propose jointly training them to simulate interactions among multiple people.
